title: A protocol for imaging calcium and chloride in C. elegans glia upon touch stimulation
protocol: Place a 15 cm length borosilicate capillary glass in the Sutter P-1000 micropipette puller.
Fabricate two needles using specified settings on the Sutter P-1000 puller.
Heat the tip of the needles to melt it into the shape of a bulb of 10–20 μm using the fire polisher.
Add 1 g agarose to 50 mL of imaging buffer (2% w/v) and heat the mixture in a microwave until fully dissolved.
Allow the heated agarose mix to cool for 2–3 minutes at room temperature while preparing coverslips.
Use cooled agarose to create slightly thicker pads that stay moist longer.
Seal the flask with parafilm after cooling and store at 4°C for up to a month.
Reheat stored agarose using reduced microwave power to avoid water evaporation.
Place ∼25 18 × 18 mm cover glass on a flat surface.
Add one drop (∼100 μL) of 2% agarose on the center of each slide using a disposable Pasteur pipette.
Gently lay down a 22 × 22 mm cover glass on top of the agarose drop while it is still in liquid form.
Carefully separate the larger cover glass from the smaller one with a razorblade, ensuring the pad remains on the small glass.
Store the pads in a 150 mm petri dish immediately.
Place a wet wipe tissue in the middle of the dish to keep the pads moist.
Store the pads with the wet wipe tissue at 4°C for up to a week.
Check for dryness before using the pads.
Make fresh pads every 2-3 days for better performance.
Pick a fluorescent young adult worm with an eyelash and place it on the agarose pad.
Dip the tip of a probe into the glue (Gluture).
Place a drop of glue on the pad near the tail of the worm.
Touch the tail of the worm with the glued probe to immobilize it.
Dip the probe in the drop of glue and start gluing one side of the worm until the glue reaches the tip of the nose but does not cover it.
Place the cover glass containing the glued worm into the calcium imaging chamber.
Fill the chamber with imaging solution.
Remove air bubbles from the worm's nose using a probe.
Manipulate the probe carefully to avoid stimulating the worm's nose.
Open micromanager or equivalent microscope control software.
Open PIMikroMove or similar probe movement control software.
Use bright field illumination and low magnification objective to find the worm.
Position the worm so that the tip of its nose faces the probe at the desired angle.
Focus on the tip of the worm's nose.
Move the probe close to the tip of the nose.
Adjust the angle of action for optimal results.
Retract the probe 150 μm for 30 seconds.
Push the probe forward 200 μm.
Retract the probe 200 μm.
Set the Z axis position critically to activate the cell of interest effectively.
Use the two black parallel lines at the mouth of the worm as a reference point.
Adjust the focus on the computer view.
Position the probe as close as possible to the nose without touching it.
Choose emission and excitation filters for GCaMP-6s in AMsh glia.
Use YFP excitation filter with no emission filters for GCaMP-6s.
Select CFP excitation filter and CFP, YFP emission filters for SuperClomeleon.
Focus on the cell of interest under fluorescence.
Adjust exposure time based on experiment requirements.
Use 50 ms exposure time for AMsh glial cells expressing GCaMP-6s.
Use 20 ms exposure time for chloride imaging with SuperClomeleon in AMsh.
Increase exposure time to 100 ms for ASH neurons.
Start recording using the specified mechanical stimulation protocol.
Retract probe by 150 μm for 30 seconds.
Push probe forward by 200 μm after retraction.
Retract probe again by 200 μm, ready for subsequent touch stimulations.
